<reason>A high-quality, tightly joined debate that narrowed to one interpretive question: is CON's "bespoke" regime the motion's alternative or PRO's regime renamed? PRO won that question on the motion as written. CON built its case plank by plank out of broker-dealer protections (segregation, capital, conflicts separation, exams, a SIPC-style backstop) and then, in B4.2, conceded the result "is not light by any honest definition" — which means CON was no longer defending the "distinct lightly supervised category" the proposition names. PRO also neutralized CON's strongest threshold objection (classification is symmetric since CON admits securities law already reaches promoter tokens and "someone must classify every token"), handled the Bitcoin/Ether issue via ordinary dual registration, and in A4.4 named securities-specific machinery (treasury/vesting/insider disclosure, best execution, suitability, house-market-maker ban, wash-trade surveillance) that CON never rebutted. CON scored real points — the SIPC asset-gating argument went unanswered, the FTX solvent affiliate was CFTC- not SEC-regulated, and the "annex every alternative" charge was sharp — but these show PRO's charter is imperfect rather than that a lightly supervised category is preferable. CON's clipped rebuttal was a minor execution cost. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 (A3.1) forcing CON to name a protection its regime removes, followed by CON's answer "None that protects" and the admission the regime is "not light" (B4.1–B4.2), which PRO's closing turned into the decisive line: CON built the house and denied it was a house because of the nameplate.</best_rebuttal>
